awd_titl_txt: Planning Grant: Strategic planning of The Pinelands Research Institute
awd_abstract_narration:
An award is made to the Pinelands Research Institute to support the establishment and initial activities of the Institute Advisory Board and development of a 10-year strategic plan for the Institute. These funds will help bring together a group of scholars, stakeholders and community members, all dedicated to research and education aimed at understanding and protecting the unique pine barrens ecosystem in New Jersey. The project will support education, enrichment, and environmental conservation activities for all the citizens of southern New Jersey, from K-12 students through senior volunteers. Among the planned activities will be the first Institute Bioblitz, which will be held in September 2025.
 
Pine barrens ecosystems are globally distributed but quite rare. The Pinelands of New Jersey are a highly unique and preserved pine barrens ecosystem sandwiched in the middle of two of the largest urban centers on earth (New York City and Philadelphia). Indeed, the Pinelands National Reserve encompasses 1.1 million acres of minimally developed forest making it especially valuable for research. Currently, there is no other residential, terrestrial biological research station in all of New Jersey, and the newly established Pinelands Research Institute will fill a critical research need by providing a residential and remote facility for both fundamental and applied ecological research in a distinctly valuable and rare ecosystem. The Institute is expected to make critical contributions to seminal research in areas, such as terrestrial, soil and forest ecology, the evolution of rare and endemic species, fire management and conservation, pine barrens hydrology, and anthropogenic influences.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
The planning grant supported the development of a strategic plan for the newly established Pinelands Research Institute in the pine barrens of New Jersey. We successfully accomplished multiple major initiatives under the support of this planning grant. Primarily, we assembled and convened our Advisory Board. The Board includes members from academia, government and non-profit conservation researchers and practitioners. Over the course of the first year, the Advisory Board met onsite at the Institute and supported the development of the Strategic Plan.  The Plan outlines three primary initiatives of the early years of the Institute. The development of 1. physical capital 2. human capital through research fellowships to work onsite as well as working groups and 3. educational programs for students of all stages and ages. Most importantly, the Plan establishes the mission and goals of the Institute as an inclusive research and learning center focused on rare ecosystems and pine barrens habitats specifically.

 

In addition to the development of the Plan, the planning grant has funded numerous activities that directly support the mission of the Institute. These activities include hosting seminars related to the science of the pine barrens, hosting a science forum in which researchers from all career stages present their work, and most recently, a researcher open house where numerous scholars toured our forests and facilities. These events are establishing the Institute as a regional center for science, research and understanding. All events have been equally attended by academics and scholars as well as the public. The benefits of these seminars and outreach activities go beyond a day of learning. These events support existing and new collaborations among regional researchers and the Institute. As an outcome of these events, we have established research partnerships with faculty from Rutgers, Princeton and Rowan Universities and Stockton College. In addition, we further strengthened our relationship with the scientists of the US Forest Service Silas Little Experimental Forest. Indeed, with support from this grant, we installed weather monitoring equipment that will inform regional climate data acquisition in south New Jersey.

 

The first summer of field research at the Institute was quite productive. Students and faculty PIs carried out projects centered at the Institute and funds from the planning grant indirectly supported their work. However, funds from this planning grant directly supported travel to the Organization for Biological Field Stations (Schoodic Institute in Maine, September 2026) meeting for Dr. Krumins and two of the Institute’s summer researchers. The research students presented posters at the meeting describing their research and the outcomes. Both projects set the foundation for further research questions in fire ecology and management as well as mycorrhizal colonization in the rare Atlantic White Cedar forests of our campus. Manuscript preparation is in progress on the mycorrhizal findings, and plans are underway now to extend both projects in the future.
